t: In any proceeding brought under section 407 or 408 in which the application of a regulation issued under this Act is at issue, the court may review the validity of the regulation in accordance with the provisions of subparagraphs (A) through (D) of section 706(2) of title 5, United States Code, except that with respect to regulations approved by a joint resolution under section 304(c), only the provisions of section 706(2)(B) of title 5, United States Code, shall apply. If the court determines that the regulation is invalid, the court shall apply, to the extent necessary and appropriate, the most relevant substantive executive agency regulation promulgated to implement the statutory provisions with respect to which the invalid regulation was issued. Except as provided in this section, the validity of regulations issued under this Act is not subject to judicial review.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that letting a court review a regulation's validity grants a right to sue over a federal decision. But the section creates no new cause of action: it only sets the scope of review inside proceedings already brought under sections 407 or 408 and otherwise bars judicial review of the regulations. Describing and limiting litigation is not the same as granting an outside party a right to challenge a federal decision, and the section provides no comment period, hearing, advisory body, or consultation with outside parties.
fable.s: Except as provided in this section, the validity of regulations issued under this Act is not subject to judicial review.

qwen_block.w: The section explicitly grants the right to bring a proceeding (a lawsuit) to challenge the validity of federal regulations. The definition states that participation includes 'the ability to sue the government over a decision.' Although the text describes the scope of judicial review, it inherently grants the standing/right to an outside party to initiate such a proceeding, which constitutes participation. The tempting 'No' reading might focus on the procedural limits of the review (e.g., specific subsections of APA), but the core mechanism is the right to sue.
qwen_block.s: In any proceeding brought under section 407 or 408 in which the application of a regulation issued under this Act is at issue, the court may review the validity of the regulation

opus.w: This section only sets the standard a court uses to review regulations in proceedings that other sections (407 and 408) already authorize, and it narrows judicial review rather than granting anyone a new right to sue. Describing or limiting litigation is not participation under the definition. The reference to 'regulations issued under this Act' points to rules made elsewhere and does not grant rulemaking authority here, so no outside party is brought into a federal decision.
opus.s: Except as provided in this section, the validity of regulations issued under this Act is not subject to judicial review.
opus.b:
1. **The tempting reading:** The section talks about a court reviewing whether a regulation is valid, which can look like giving an outside party a right to challenge a federal decision. It also mentions "regulations issued under this Act," which can look like a grant of rulemaking power.

2. **Why it fails:** The section does not create any right to sue. It only sets the standard of review inside lawsuits that sections 407 and 408 already authorize. It also limits review: "Except as provided in this section, the validity of regulations issued under this Act is not subject to judicial review." The definition says that describing or limiting litigation is not the same as granting a right to sue. The mention of regulations refers to rules issued elsewhere in the Act; it is not a grant of rulemaking authority. Also, the cross-references point to the Congressional Accountability Act, where those suits are brought by legislative-branch employees, who are inside the federal government.

qwen_chat.w: This section defines the scope and standard of judicial review for regulations, specifying which provisions of the Administrative Procedure Act apply. It does not grant a new right to sue or require consultation with outside parties. The definition explicitly excludes 'a court's jurisdiction, venue, or the statute-of-limitations period for suits' and notes that 'limiting or describing litigation is not the same as GRANTING an outside party a right to sue.' Since this text only describes the mechanics of review rather than initiating participation or granting access, it is labeled No.
qwen_chat.s: Except as provided in this section, the validity of regulations issued under this Act is not subject to judicial review.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the text mentions "proceeding brought under section 407 or 408" and "judicial review," it implies an outside party's right to sue, which is listed as a form of participation. However, the definition explicitly states that "a court's jurisdiction, venue, or the statute-of-limitations period for suits - limiting or describing litigation is not the same as GRANTING an outside party a right to sue a decision." This section describes the *scope* and *standard* of judicial review (what the court can review and how), rather than granting the initial right to bring the suit. The right to sue is presumably granted elsewhere (in sections 407/408). Therefore, this section itself does not constitute participation; it defines the legal boundaries of existing litigation.
